In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[p-adic analysis|{{math|''p''}}-adic analysis]], the '''Artin–Hasse exponential''', introduced by [[Emil Artin]] and [[Helmut Hasse]] in 1928,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Artin |first1=Emil |last2=Hasse |first2=Helmut |date=1928 |title=Die beiden Ergänzungssätze zum Reziprozitätsgesetz der {{math|''l''{{sup|''n''}}}}-ten Potenzreste im Körper der {{math|''l''{{sup|''n''}}}}-ten Einheitswurzeln |journal=Abhandlungen Hamburg |volume=6 |pages=146–162|doi=10.1007/BF02940607 |jfm= 54.0191.05}}</ref> is the [[power series]] given by

:<math> E_p(x) = \exp\left(x + \frac{x^p}{p} + \frac{x^{p^2}}{p^2} + \frac{x^{p^3}}{p^3} +\cdots\right).</math>

==Motivation==

One motivation for considering this series to be analogous to the exponential function comes from infinite products. In the ring of formal power series <math>\Q[[x]]</math> we have the identity

::<math>e^x = \prod_{n \geq 1}(1-x^n)^{-\mu(n)/n},</math>

where <math>\mu</math> is the [[Möbius function]]. This identity can be verified by showing that the logarithmic derivatives of both sides are equal and that both sides have the same constant term. Similarly, one can verify a product expansion for the Artin–Hasse exponential:

::<math>E_p(x) = \prod_{(p,n)=1}(1-x^n)^{-\mu(n)/n}.</math>

So passing from a product over all <math>n</math> to a product over only <math>n</math> [[coprime integers|coprime]] to <math>p</math>, which is a typical operation in <math>p</math>-adic analysis, leads from <math>e^x</math> to <math>E_p(x)</math>.

== Properties ==

The coefficients of <math>E_p(x)</math> are rational. We can use either formula for <math>E_p(x)</math> to prove that, unlike <math>e^x</math>, all of its coefficients are <math>p</math>-integral; in other words, the denominators of the coefficients of <math>E_p(x)</math> are not divisible by <math>p</math>.

A first proof uses the definition of <math>E_p(x)</math> and '''Dwork's lemma''', which says that a power series <math>f(x)</math> with rational coefficients has <math>p</math>-integral coefficients if and only if
:<math>\frac{f(x^p)}{f(x)^p}\equiv 1\mod p\Z_p[[x]].</math>
When <math>f(x)=E_p(x)</math>, we have
:<math>\frac{f(x^p)}{f(x)^p} = e^{-px},</math>
where the constant term is 1 and all higher coefficients are in <math>p\Z_p</math>.

A second proof comes from the [[infinite product]] for <math>E_p(x)</math>: each exponent <math>-\mu(n)/n</math> for <math>n</math> not divisible by <math>p</math> is a <math>p</math>-integral, and when a [[rational number]] <math>a</math> is <math>p</math>-integral, all coefficients in the binomial expansion of <math>(1-x^n)^a</math> are <math>p</math>-integral by <math>p</math>-adic continuity of the [[binomial coefficient]] polynomials
:<math>\frac{t!}{k!(t-k)!}</math>
in <math>t</math> together with their obvious integrality when <math>t</math> is a nonnegative integer (<math>a</math> is a <math>p</math>-adic limit of nonnegative integers). Thus, each factor in the product of <math>E_p(x)</math> has <math>p</math>-integral coefficients, so <math>E_p(x)</math> itself has <math>p</math>-integral coefficients.

The <math>p</math>-integral series expansion has [[radius of convergence]] 1.

==Combinatorial interpretation==
The Artin–Hasse exponential is the [[generating function]] for the probability that a uniformly randomly selected element of the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math> has <math>p</math>-power order (the number of which is denoted by <math>t_{p,n}</math>):

:<math>E_p(x)=\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac{t_{p,n}}{n!}x^n.</math>

This gives a third proof that the coefficients of <math>E_p(x)</math> are <math>p</math>-integral, using the [[Frobenius's theorem (group theory)|theorem of Frobenius]] that in a [[finite group]] of order divisible by <math>d</math> the number of elements of order dividing <math>d</math> is also divisible by <math>d</math>. Apply this theorem to the <math>n</math>th symmetric group with <math>d</math> equal to the highest power of <math>p</math> dividing <math>n!</math>.

More generally, for any topologically finitely generated profinite group <math>G</math> there is an identity
:<math>\exp\bigg(\sum_{H \subset G} x^{[G:H]}/[G:H]\bigg)=\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac{a_{G,n}}{n!}x^n,</math>
where <math>H</math> runs over open subgroups of <math>G</math> of finite index (there are finitely many of each index since <math>G</math> is topologically finitely generated) and <math>a_{G,n}</math> is the number of continuous homomorphisms from <math>G</math> to <math>S_n</math>.

Two special cases are worth noting. Firstly, if <math>G</math> is the <math>p</math>-adic integers, it has exactly one open subgroup of each <math>p</math>-power index and a continuous homomorphism from <math>G</math> to <math>S_n</math> is essentially the same thing as choosing an element of <math>p</math>-power order in <math>S_n</math>, so we have recovered the above combinatorial interpretation of the Taylor coefficients in the Artin–Hasse exponential series. 

Secondly, if <math>G</math> is a finite group, then the sum in the exponential is a finite sum running over all subgroups of <math>G</math>, and continuous homomorphisms from <math>G</math> to <math>S_n</math> are simply homomorphisms from <math>G</math> to <math>S_n</math>. The result in this case is due to Wohlfahrt.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wohlfahrt |first=Klaus |date=1977 |title=Über einen Satz von Dey und die Modulgruppe |journal=Archiv der Mathematik |volume=29 |pages=455–457|doi=10.1007/BF01220437 |mr=0507036}}</ref>

The special case when <math>G</math> is a finite [[cyclic group]] is due to Chowla, Herstein, and Scott (1952),{{Citation needed|date=October 2025}} and takes the form
:<math>\exp\bigg(\sum_{d|m} x^d/d\bigg)=\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac{a_{m,n}}{n!}x^n,</math>
where <math>a_{m,n}</math> is the number of solutions to <math>g^m=1</math> in ''S<sub>n</sub>''.

David Roberts provided a natural combinatorial link between the Artin–Hasse exponential and the regular exponential in the spirit of the ergodic perspective (linking the <math>p</math>-adic and regular norms over the rationals) by showing that the Artin–Hasse exponential is also the generating function for the probability that an element of the symmetric group is [[unipotent]] in [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] <math>p</math>, whereas the regular exponential is the probability that an element of the same group is unipotent in characteristic zero.{{citation needed|date=May 2015}}

==Conjectures==

At the 2002 [[PROMYS]] program, Keith Conrad conjectured that the coefficients of <math>E_p(x)</math> are uniformly distributed in the  [[p-adic number|{{math|''p''}}-adic]] integers with respect to the normalized [[Haar measure]], with supporting computational evidence. The problem is still open.

Dinesh Thakur has also posed the problem of whether the Artin–Hasse exponential reduced mod <math>p</math> is transcendental over <math>\mathbb{F}_p(x)</math>.
